questions.q: Why can Git flag a conflict in package.xml even when two developers added genuinely unrelated components?
options: Because package.xml cannot be tracked by Git at all
Because Git's conflict detection works line-by-line on text and has no understanding that XML elements can be reordered without changing meaning
Because Salesforce encrypts all metadata files
Because package.xml always requires manual regeneration
questions.explain: Metadata is XML, and Git compares it as plain text line by line — it has no semantic understanding of XML, so two unrelated additions near the same spot in a list can still register as a conflict.

questions.q: When two branches each add a different, legitimately needed <members> entry to the same package.xml list, what's usually the correct resolution?
options: Pick whichever side's entry came first alphabetically and discard the other
Delete the entire <types> block to avoid the conflict
Always keep only the version from main
Keep the union of both sides' entries (removing only genuine duplicates), not just one branch's list
questions.explain: In most real cases both sides added separate, legitimate components — the correct resolution is the union of both lists, not picking one side and discarding the other's intended addition.

questions.q: Why are Profile and Permission Set metadata files especially prone to false-positive conflicts?
options: They list permissions as long ordered sequences, so two unrelated permission grants often land near the same physical lines purely due to list ordering
They cannot be stored in source format at all
They are stored as binary files, not XML
Salesforce blocks them from being committed to Git
questions.explain: Because permissions are listed in a long, ordering-dependent sequence, two logically unrelated changes (granting access to two different fields) can still touch physically nearby lines, producing a conflict that isn't a real logical disagreement.

questions.q: What is a validation-only (check-only) deploy used for after resolving a metadata conflict?
options: To permanently save the resolved metadata to production immediately
To delete the conflicting branch
To run all of Salesforce's deploy validation, including required tests, without actually saving the change to the org — confirming the resolution is actually correct
To automatically generate a new package.xml
questions.explain: A validation-only deploy runs the full validation Salesforce would perform (including test execution) without committing the change to the org — much stronger evidence of correctness than just confirming the XML parses.

questions.q: What is a git merge driver, as described in this lesson, used for?
options: Automatically writing commit messages
Configuring, via .gitattributes, structure-aware merge logic for a specific file type instead of Git's default line-based text merge
Preventing any file from ever being merged
Converting metadata API format to source format
questions.explain: A merge driver, set up via .gitattributes, tells Git to merge a specific file type (like Profile XML) using logic aware of its structure, reducing false-positive conflicts compared to Git's default line-based approach.
